questions.stem: What does classification mean in biology?
options: Counting how many organisms live in an area
Giving every organism a common name
Deciding which organisms are most useful
Sorting organisms into groups based on shared features
questions.explanation: Classification groups organisms by shared characteristics. Counting organisms is sampling, and usefulness plays no part in scientific grouping.

questions.stem: Which are the five kingdoms used in the traditional classification system?
options: Mammals, reptiles, birds, fish and amphibians
Predators, prey, producers, decomposers and parasites
Animals, plants, fungi, protists and bacteria
Animals, plants, insects, fish and birds
questions.explanation: The five kingdoms sort all life at the broadest level. Mammals and reptiles are much smaller groups within the animal kingdom.

questions.stem: Which kingdom do mushrooms belong to?
questions.explanation: Fungi have cell walls but no chlorophyll, so they cannot photosynthesise — they feed on dead or living material instead.
questions.teaching:
Living things are sorted into kingdoms, and the boundaries are drawn on how an organism gets its energy and what its cells are like.

Plants make their own food using light. Animals eat other organisms and can move about. A third group has cell walls like plants but cannot photosynthesise — instead it absorbs nutrients from dead or living material around it, digesting food outside its body and taking the products in. Mushrooms, moulds and yeasts all belong there. Being stationary and growing from the ground makes them look plant-like, which is exactly why they were classified as plants for centuries.

questions.stem: What are the two parts of an organism's scientific name?
questions.explanation: Binomial names are genus then species, like Homo sapiens. The genus is capitalised and the species is not.

questions.stem: What is a vertebrate?
options: An animal with a hard outer shell
An animal that lives in water
questions.explanation: Vertebrates have an internal backbone. Plenty of invertebrates lay eggs and live in water, so those features do not define the group.

questions.stem: Which of these is an invertebrate?
questions.explanation: Snails have no backbone, so they are invertebrates. Frogs, sharks and snakes all have one, even though their body plans look very different from each other.
questions.teaching:
The two words look like opposites and one is simply the other with a prefix meaning 'not'.

The dividing line is a backbone — a column of vertebrae running down the back. Animals with one include fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals, and they make up a surprisingly small share of all animal species. Everything else falls on the other side: insects, spiders, crustaceans, worms, molluscs, jellyfish and corals, which together account for the vast majority of animal species on Earth. Size is no guide at all — a giant squid has no backbone.

questions.stem: Which group do animals that feed their young on milk belong to?
questions.explanation: Producing milk is the defining mammal feature. Fur and warm blood are typical too, but milk is the reliable test.

questions.stem: What is a species?
options: Any group of animals that look similar
All the organisms living in one habitat
A group of organisms of the same colour
A group of organisms that can breed together to produce fertile offspring
questions.explanation: The fertile-offspring test is what defines a species. Looking similar is not enough — some very similar species cannot interbreed.
questions.teaching:
"Looks similar" turns out to be a poor definition, because it fails in both directions. Great Danes and chihuahuas look nothing alike and are one species; some butterflies are indistinguishable and are several.

Biologists use a breeding test instead. The key detail is the word "fertile": a horse and a donkey can produce a mule, and the mule is healthy, but it cannot itself have offspring. So horses and donkeys stay separate. That fertility requirement is what the whole definition turns on, and it is what makes speciation identifiable — once two populations can no longer produce fertile young together, the split is complete.

questions.stem: What is a dichotomous key?
options: A list of every species in a habitat
A diagram showing what eats what
A tool that identifies an organism through a series of paired choices
questions.explanation: 'Dichotomous' means splitting in two: at each step you choose between two statements until you reach a name.

questions.stem: Which feature do all arthropods share?
options: A hard exoskeleton and jointed legs
questions.explanation: Exoskeleton plus jointed legs defines arthropods. Eight legs applies only to arachnids, and many arthropods have no wings.

questions.stem: How many legs does an insect have?
questions.explanation: Insects have six legs and usually three body parts. Eight legs means an arachnid, such as a spider.
questions.teaching:
Arthropods are told apart by counting, and the counts are worth having by heart because so many questions depend on them.

The group in question here has a body in three parts: head, thorax and abdomen. Legs attach only to the middle section, one pair per segment, and there are three segments — so counting the pairs on the thorax gives you the total. This group also has one pair of antennae and, usually, wings. Arachnids differ on every count: two body sections, no antennae, no wings, and one extra pair of legs.

questions.stem: Which group do frogs and toads belong to?
questions.explanation: Amphibians typically begin life in water with gills and move onto land as adults. Reptiles have scales and lay shelled eggs on land.
questions.teaching:
Vertebrates split into five classes, and each is defined by a small set of features rather than by general appearance.

Fish have gills and live in water throughout life. Reptiles have dry scaly skin and lay shelled eggs on land. Birds have feathers. Mammals have hair and feed young on milk. The remaining class is the one with a life cycle in two stages: eggs laid in water, larvae with gills, then adults with lungs and moist skin that must stay damp. Frogs, toads, newts and salamanders belong there, and their dependence on water is why they are so vulnerable to drought.

questions.stem: What do reptiles have covering their skin?
questions.explanation: Dry scaly skin reduces water loss, which is one reason reptiles manage in dry habitats. Amphibians have moist skin instead.

questions.stem: Which kingdom includes organisms that make their own food using light?
questions.explanation: Plants photosynthesise. Some bacteria and protists do too, but the plant kingdom is defined by it.

questions.stem: Why do scientists use scientific names instead of common names?
options: Scientific names describe what the organism eats
Common names vary between places and languages, so they can be ambiguous
questions.explanation: One animal can have many common names in different regions, and the same common name can be used for different animals. A binomial name is unique.

questions.stem: Two organisms look almost identical but cannot produce fertile offspring together. What follows?
options: One of them is not alive
They must be in different kingdoms
questions.explanation: The species definition rests on fertile offspring, not appearance. Different species can look nearly identical.

questions.stem: A student uses a key and reaches a dead end with no matching option. What is the most likely problem?
options: The organism belongs to no kingdom
They made a wrong choice at an earlier step
The key must include every species on Earth
questions.explanation: Keys are sequential, so one wrong turn sends you down a branch that cannot fit. Retracing the steps usually fixes it.

questions.stem: Why is a whale classified as a mammal and not a fish?
options: It breathes air with lungs and feeds its young on milk
questions.explanation: Classification follows shared ancestry and body features, not habitat. Living in water and having fins are shared with fish through similar lifestyles, not relatedness.

questions.stem: Which pair of organisms is most closely related?
options: Two organisms in the same class
Two organisms in the same phylum
Two organisms in the same genus
Two organisms in the same kingdom
questions.explanation: The smaller the shared group, the closer the relationship. Genus is much narrower than class, phylum or kingdom.

questions.stem: A newly found organism is single-celled with no nucleus. Which kingdom does it belong to?
questions.explanation: No nucleus means prokaryote, which places it with bacteria. Protists are single-celled but do have a nucleus.

questions.stem: Why do biologists now use DNA evidence in classification?
options: DNA similarity shows how closely organisms are related more reliably than appearance
DNA is easier to see than body features
DNA tells you what an organism eats
DNA changes with the habitat an organism lives in
questions.explanation: Unrelated organisms can look alike if they live similar lives. DNA comparisons reveal ancestry that appearance can disguise.

questions.stem: Which feature would place an animal in the bird group with most confidence?
questions.explanation: Feathers are unique to birds. Some birds cannot fly, many other animals lay eggs, and other animals stand on two legs.

questions.stem: A student groups animals into 'things that fly' — bats, birds and moths. Why isn't this scientific classification?
options: They share a way of moving, not ancestry or body structure
Only birds should be grouped at all
questions.explanation: Scientific groups are built on shared ancestry and structural features. Flight evolved separately in insects, birds and bats.

questions.stem: Which sequence goes from the largest group to the smallest?
options: Kingdom, class, phylum, family, order, genus, species
Phylum, kingdom, class, order, family, species, genus
Kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species
Species, genus, family, order, class, phylum, kingdom
questions.explanation: Kingdom is the broadest and species the narrowest. The middle order — class before order before family — is the part most often muddled.

questions.stem: Two beetles are given the names Carabus violaceus and Carabus problematicus. What does this tell you?
options: One is a beetle and one is not
They are different species in the same genus
They are the same species with two names
questions.explanation: A shared first word means a shared genus; the different second words mark them as separate species.

questions.stem: Why can classification systems change over time?
options: New evidence, especially from DNA, can show relationships were misjudged
Scientists get bored of the old names
Organisms evolve into new kingdoms each century
Common names change, so scientific ones must follow
questions.explanation: Classification is a scientific model, and models are revised when better evidence appears. Fungi were once grouped with plants for exactly this reason.

questions.stem: An animal has moist skin, lays jelly-covered eggs in water, and has young with gills. Which group is it?
questions.explanation: The two-stage life cycle, moist skin and jelly-covered eggs are all amphibian features. Fish do not leave the water as adults.

questions.stem: Which question would work best as the first step of a dichotomous key for animals?
options: Does it live near my school?
questions.explanation: A good key step is objective and splits the group roughly in two. Opinions and local details cannot be checked by another person.

questions.stem: Australia has many marsupials. What distinguishes them from other mammals?
options: Their young are born very undeveloped and continue growing in a pouch
questions.explanation: Marsupials are mammals, so they do produce milk. The egg-laying mammals are the monotremes — the platypus and echidnas.

questions.stem: Dolphins and sharks have similar streamlined bodies but are not closely related. What does this show?
options: One of them has been classified incorrectly
Similar environments can produce similar features in unrelated groups
They must belong to the same class
Appearance is the most reliable guide to relatedness
questions.explanation: This is convergent evolution: the same problem — moving fast through water — produces similar solutions in separate lineages. It is exactly why appearance alone misleads.

questions.stem: Why is the definition of a species harder to apply to bacteria?
options: Bacteria all belong to one species
Bacteria reproduce asexually, so the fertile-offspring test does not apply
Bacteria are too small to name
questions.explanation: The breeding test needs two parents. Bacteria divide on their own and also swap genes between types, so species boundaries are defined differently for them.

questions.stem: Two organisms share a phylum but not a class. Which statement is correct?
options: They are more closely related than two organisms in the same genus
They share some basic body plan features but differ substantially
questions.explanation: Sharing a broad group means sharing broad features only. Same-genus organisms are far more closely related.

questions.stem: Why are viruses usually left out of the five-kingdom system?
options: They are not made of cells and cannot carry out life processes alone
They are too small to classify
They belong to the bacteria kingdom
questions.explanation: The kingdoms classify cellular life. Viruses have genes but no cells and no independent metabolism, so they sit outside the system.

questions.stem: A key identifies an unknown plant as a species not previously recorded in the area. What is the best next step?
options: Check the identification against another source and record where and when it was found
Assume the key is wrong and discard the result
Conclude a new species has been discovered
questions.explanation: A surprising result needs verification and a documented record. Range extensions are common; new species are rare, and neither claim rests on a single key run.

questions.stem: Which evidence would best support moving a species into a different genus?
options: DNA comparisons showing it is more closely related to members of the other genus
It lives in the same habitat as the other genus
It is the same colour as the other genus
It is easier to remember that way
questions.explanation: Genus membership reflects evolutionary relatedness, which DNA measures directly. Habitat and colour can be shared by unrelated organisms.

questions.stem: Fungi were once classified with plants. Which discovery most justified separating them?
options: Fungi cannot photosynthesise and their cell walls are made of chitin, not cellulose
questions.explanation: Feeding method and wall chemistry are fundamental differences. Growing in soil and using spores are shared with some plants and so do not separate them.

questions.stem: A student argues that classification is 'just opinion' because systems have changed. What is the best response?
options: Only DNA evidence counts as science
Systems change because they are tested against new evidence, which is how science works
questions.explanation: Revision in response to evidence is a strength, not a weakness. Multiple lines of evidence — anatomy, development and DNA — constrain the groupings.

questions.stem: Why does classifying organisms help scientists studying an unfamiliar species?
options: It tells you exactly how many individuals exist
It removes the need for further observation
Its group predicts likely features, needs and relationships before it is fully studied
It guarantees the species is harmless
questions.explanation: Classification is a predictive tool: knowing something is a mammal tells you a lot before you have observed it. It guides further study rather than replacing it.

questions.stem: Which pair of features would a key use to separate two very similar grass species reliably?
options: Colour, which changes through the season
Measurable, consistent structures such as seed head shape and leaf width
Height, since one may be taller on the day
questions.explanation: Key steps need features that stay the same regardless of growing conditions. Height, colour and health vary with water, light and season.

questions.stem: What is taxonomy?
options: The study of how animals behave
The study of where organisms live
The science of naming and classifying organisms
questions.explanation: Taxonomy is naming and grouping. Behaviour is ethology and distribution is biogeography.

questions.stem: Which kingdom do single-celled organisms with a nucleus, such as amoebae, belong to?
questions.explanation: Protists are eukaryotic and mostly single-celled. Bacteria are single-celled too but have no nucleus.

questions.stem: How is a genus name written?
options: In lower case with no italics
With a capital letter and in italics
questions.explanation: The convention is Genus capitalised, species lower case, both italicised — for example Eucalyptus regnans.

questions.stem: Which group of vertebrates has feathers?
questions.explanation: Feathers are unique to birds and are the single most reliable identifying feature of the group.
questions.teaching:
Each vertebrate class has one feature that no other class shares, and learning those single markers makes identification quick.

Hair and milk-producing glands mark one class. Dry scales and shelled eggs mark another. Gills throughout life mark a third. Moist skin and a two-stage life cycle mark a fourth. And one class has a body covering found in no other animal alive today — a structure that provides insulation and, in most members, flight. It is also the clearest evidence linking that class back to dinosaurs, since fossils show the covering appearing well before flight did.

questions.stem: What do we call an animal that keeps a steady body temperature using its own heat?
questions.explanation: Endotherms — birds and mammals — generate their own heat. Ectotherms rely on their surroundings.

questions.stem: Which group do spiders belong to?
questions.explanation: Arachnids have eight legs and two body parts. Insects have six legs and three body parts.
questions.teaching:
Two arthropod groups are constantly confused, and there are three quick tests that separate them.

One group has a body in three sections — head, thorax and abdomen — plus antennae, and usually wings. The other has the head and thorax fused into a single section, so only two parts are visible, no antennae at all, and never wings. It also has one more pair of legs than the first group. Spiders, scorpions, ticks and mites all belong to the second. Counting body sections is the fastest test, and looking for antennae is the next fastest.

questions.stem: Which of these is a crustacean?
questions.explanation: Crustaceans such as crabs, prawns and slaters usually have a hard shell and many pairs of limbs.
questions.teaching:
Arthropods are the largest animal group, and they are divided by body sections, legs and antennae.

Insects have three body sections and antennae. Arachnids have two sections and no antennae. A third group is mostly aquatic, has two pairs of antennae and a hard exoskeleton often reinforced with calcium carbonate, and includes crabs, prawns, lobsters, yabbies and barnacles. Sorting an unfamiliar animal means counting sections and antennae rather than going on general appearance — which is how you tell a slater from an insect.

questions.stem: What does 'biodiversity' mean?
options: The variety of living things in an area
The total number of animals in an area
The size of the largest species in an area
The amount of water available in an area
questions.explanation: Biodiversity is about variety — how many different kinds — not simply how many individuals.
questions.teaching:
The word combines "biological" and "diversity", and the second half is the part that matters.

It measures variety rather than quantity, and it works at several levels: the number of different species in an area, the genetic variation within each species, and the range of ecosystems present. A wheat paddock can hold millions of individual plants and have very low biodiversity, while a patch of remnant bushland next to it has far fewer plants and far more. Australia is one of seventeen megadiverse countries, with a high proportion of species found nowhere else — which is why habitat loss here matters globally.

questions.stem: Which characteristic do all living things share?
options: They move from place to place
questions.explanation: Respiration is universal. Photosynthesis, movement and backbones each apply to only some groups.

questions.stem: What are the seven life processes often remembered as MRS GREN?
options: Motion, reaction, size, growth, response, energy, nutrients
Movement, reproduction, sight, growth, respiration, eating, nutrition
Metabolism, respiration, sensing, genetics, reproduction, energy, nutrition
Movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion, nutrition
questions.explanation: MRS GREN is the standard mnemonic. It is the checklist for deciding whether something is alive.

questions.stem: Which group of plants reproduces using spores rather than seeds?
questions.explanation: Ferns and mosses release spores. Conifers make seeds in cones and flowering plants make them in flowers.

questions.stem: What is a common name?
options: An everyday name for an organism, which can vary between places
The name of the genus only
questions.explanation: Common names are local and inconsistent — the same fish has different names in different states.

questions.stem: Which group includes animals with a soft body, often protected by a shell?
questions.explanation: Snails, mussels and octopuses are molluscs. Arthropods have a hard exoskeleton and jointed legs instead.

questions.stem: How many legs does an arachnid have?
questions.explanation: Eight legs is the arachnid signature. Six legs means an insect.
questions.teaching:
Two arthropod groups differ by exactly one pair of legs, which is why questions pair them so often.

Insects have three body sections, antennae, and three pairs of legs attached to the middle section. The other group has the head and thorax fused into one, no antennae, no wings, and one pair of legs more than insects do. Spiders, scorpions, ticks and mites all belong there. If you can remember the insect figure, you can work this one out by adding a pair rather than memorising it separately.

questions.stem: Which group do worms with segmented bodies belong to?
questions.explanation: Earthworms and leeches are annelids, recognisable by the rings that segment the body.

questions.stem: What is an organism's habitat?
options: The particular place where it lives
The group it is classified in
questions.explanation: A habitat is a place — a rock pool, a hollow log, a reef.

questions.stem: Which two kingdoms contain organisms that all have cell walls but never chloroplasts?
questions.explanation: Fungi and bacteria have walls but do not photosynthesise. Plants have walls and chloroplasts; animals have neither.

questions.stem: Which group do platypuses and echidnas belong to?
questions.explanation: Monotremes are the egg-laying mammals. They still produce milk, which is why they are mammals.

questions.stem: What is a key step in a dichotomous key called?
questions.explanation: Each step is a pair of mutually exclusive statements. Offering three options would break the 'di-' in dichotomous.

questions.stem: Which group of animals has scales and lays soft-shelled eggs on land?
questions.explanation: Reptile eggs have a leathery shell and are laid on land. Bird eggs are hard-shelled, and amphibian eggs are jelly-covered and laid in water.

questions.stem: A key asks 'Does the animal have wings?' and a student is looking at an ant. What is the safest approach?
options: Check whether that species and life stage has wings, since some ants do and some do not
Answer no, because ants never have wings
Answer yes, because all insects have wings
Skip the step and move to the next one
questions.explanation: Winged and wingless forms occur within the same ant species. A key step must be applied to the specimen in front of you, not to a general impression.

questions.stem: Two organisms are placed in the same family but different genera. What can you say?
options: They are related but less closely than two members of one genus
questions.explanation: Family is a broader group than genus, so shared family means a more distant relationship.

questions.stem: A student finds an animal with a hard shell, jointed legs and a segmented body in a rock pool. Which group?
questions.explanation: Jointed legs and a hard exoskeleton put it with the arthropods; a marine one with many limbs is most likely a crustacean. Molluscs have shells but no jointed legs.

questions.stem: Why is it useful that scientific names are the same worldwide?
options: Scientists in different countries can be sure they mean the same organism
The names are easier to pronounce
It means fewer species need to be named
It shows which organisms are most useful
questions.explanation: Unambiguous communication is the whole point. A shared name removes translation and regional confusion.

questions.stem: An organism photosynthesises, is single-celled, and has a nucleus. Which kingdom?
questions.explanation: Photosynthetic single-celled eukaryotes such as Euglena are protists. The plant kingdom is multicellular.

questions.stem: Why might two organisms in the same species look quite different?
options: Variation within a species is normal, including between males and females
They must actually be different species
One of them has been misclassified
questions.explanation: Variation, including sexual dimorphism and age differences, occurs within every species. Male and female eclectus parrots look so different they were once thought to be two species.

questions.stem: What does it mean if a species is described as endemic to Australia?
options: It is found in Australia and several other countries
It occurs naturally in Australia and nowhere else
questions.explanation: Endemic means naturally restricted to one place. Koalas and platypuses are endemic to Australia; introduced species are the opposite case.

questions.stem: A key leads a student to a species, but the specimen has an extra pair of legs. What should they do?
options: Recheck the earlier steps and consider that the key may not cover this group
Assume the specimen is a new species
questions.explanation: A mismatch means either a wrong turn or a key that does not include this organism. Neither justifies recording a result you can see is wrong.

questions.stem: Why do scientists group organisms hierarchically rather than in one long list?
options: A hierarchy shows degrees of relatedness, not just names
A list would be too long to print
It lets every organism have several names
questions.explanation: Nested groups carry information: sharing a genus means much more than sharing a kingdom. A flat list carries none.

questions.stem: Which feature would NOT be useful in a dichotomous key?
options: Whether the stem is round or square
Whether the leaf edge is smooth or toothed
Whether there are five or six petals
questions.explanation: Key features must be objective and consistent. Health is a judgement and varies with conditions; the others can be checked by anyone.

questions.stem: An introduced species spreads rapidly through Australian bushland. Why is classification useful here?
options: It removes the need for field surveys
Knowing its group predicts how it reproduces and spreads, guiding control
It tells you exactly how many individuals there are
It proves the species is harmful
questions.explanation: Group membership carries predictive information about biology and life cycle. Numbers still require surveying.

questions.stem: Which statement about the five-kingdom system is correct?
options: It groups all cellular life, but modern systems often use three domains as well
It is the only system scientists have ever used
It includes viruses as a sixth kingdom
questions.explanation: The five-kingdom system remains a useful teaching model, but classification above kingdom now uses domains. Viruses remain outside it.

questions.stem: Whales were once classified with fish. What evidence best justified reclassifying them as mammals?
options: A streamlined body and fins closely matching those of sharks and other predators
Living in salt water all year and never coming onto land to feed or to breed
Being warm to the touch and swimming in groups, as many schooling fish also do
Lungs, live birth, milk production and a four-chambered heart shared with land mammals
questions.explanation: Internal anatomy and reproduction reveal ancestry that external shape disguises. This is the classic case of convergence misleading early classifiers.

questions.stem: Why can classification of extinct species be harder than for living ones?
options: Only hard parts usually survive, and interbreeding cannot be tested
Extinct species had no features worth recording
Fossils cannot be compared with living organisms
Extinct species were not related to living ones
questions.explanation: Soft tissue, behaviour and breeding are all unavailable, so the species definition has to be applied to skeletal evidence alone.

questions.stem: Which finding would most support placing two populations in the same species?
options: They are similar in size and colour
They interbreed in the wild and produce fertile offspring
They live in the same habitat
questions.explanation: The definition rests on gene flow producing fertile offspring. Shared habitat, diet and appearance can all occur between distinct species.

questions.stem: A mule is the offspring of a horse and a donkey and is infertile. What does this show?
options: Horses and donkeys are the same species
Fertility matters only when classifying plants
Horses and donkeys are separate species
questions.explanation: Offspring can be produced, but they are not fertile, so the species boundary holds. This is precisely why the definition specifies fertile offspring.

questions.stem: Why is DNA evidence sometimes described as more objective than anatomical comparison?
options: Sequence differences can be counted, while judging how similar two structures look involves interpretation
DNA comparisons require no judgement from the scientist
DNA evidence is always available for every species
questions.explanation: Counting differences is quantitative; deciding whether two bones are 'the same structure' is a judgement. DNA does change — that change is exactly what is measured.

questions.stem: Two species share a recent common ancestor. What would you predict about their DNA?
options: It will be more similar than between distantly related species
DNA similarity has no relationship to ancestry
questions.explanation: Less time since divergence means fewer accumulated differences. Identical DNA would imply no divergence at all.

questions.stem: Why is classifying a newly discovered deep-sea organism often provisional at first?
options: Initial placement rests on limited specimens and may change once DNA and more individuals are available
New organisms are always placed in a new kingdom
Deep-sea organisms are placed by depth rather than by features
questions.explanation: Science revises with evidence. A first placement from one damaged specimen is a reasonable hypothesis, not a final answer.

questions.stem: A student says 'fungi must be plants because they grow out of the ground and don't move'. Identify the flaw.
options: Plants do move from place to place
The reasoning uses superficial features rather than cell structure and feeding method
Fungi do move from place to place
Fungi do not grow out of the ground
questions.explanation: Both observations are true and both are irrelevant. Classification rests on how an organism is built and how it obtains energy.

questions.stem: Which would most challenge the current placement of a species within its genus?
options: Discovering it eats an unexpected food
DNA showing it is more closely related to a species in another genus
Finding it in a new location
Finding a larger individual than recorded
questions.explanation: Genus placement is about relatedness, so relatedness evidence challenges it. Range, size and diet do not.

questions.stem: Which group of plants produces seeds inside cones?
questions.explanation: Conifers such as pines bear seeds in cones. Flowering plants enclose seeds in fruit, and ferns and mosses use spores.

questions.stem: Which classification level sits directly above genus?
questions.explanation: The order runs kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species — so family is directly above genus.

questions.stem: What is an invertebrate's alternative to a backbone for support?
options: A cartilage rod in the tail
A ring of bony plates around the body
An exoskeleton or a fluid-filled body
questions.explanation: Arthropods use an external skeleton; worms and jellyfish use fluid pressure inside the body.

questions.stem: Which group do jellyfish and corals belong to?
questions.explanation: Cnidarians have stinging cells and a simple body with one opening.

questions.stem: What does a herbarium hold?
options: Preserved plant specimens used as reference material
questions.explanation: Herbaria store pressed, labelled plants so identifications can be checked against a physical reference.

questions.stem: Which feature is shared by all fish?
options: Gills for gas exchange in water
Scales on every part of the body
questions.explanation: All fish use gills. Sharks have cartilage rather than bone, and most fish lay eggs.

questions.stem: What is a 'type specimen'?
options: The largest known individual of a species
The first individual of a species ever seen alive
A specimen kept in a school laboratory
The individual specimen a species description is officially based on
questions.explanation: The type specimen anchors the name. If the definition of a species is disputed, this is the physical reference point.

questions.stem: What word describes an animal active at night?
questions.explanation: Nocturnal means night-active; diurnal means day-active.

questions.stem: Which term describes an organism that has been brought to an area by people?
questions.explanation: Introduced species arrive through human activity. Native species occur there naturally.

questions.stem: Which classification level would contain the greatest number of species?
questions.explanation: The broader the group, the more species it holds. Class is the broadest of these four.

questions.stem: Why can't a dichotomous key identify a species it was not written to cover?
options: Keys can identify any organism if used carefully
Every step forces a choice within a fixed set of options, so an unlisted organism reaches a wrong answer
Keys only work in the country where they were written
Keys need DNA evidence to work
questions.explanation: A key is a closed system. This is why they state their scope — 'freshwater invertebrates of south-eastern Australia', not 'all animals'.

questions.stem: Why are dichotomous keys usually built on adult features?
options: Juveniles often look very different, so adult features are more consistent
questions.explanation: A tadpole and a frog would take entirely different paths through a key. Restricting to a life stage keeps the key reliable.

questions.stem: An organism is multicellular, has no cell walls and eats other organisms. Which kingdom?
questions.explanation: No cell wall rules out fungi and plants; multicellular with ingestion is the animal pattern.

questions.stem: Why is 'insect' the wrong word for a spider?
options: Spiders have eight legs and two body parts, so they are arachnids
questions.explanation: Both are arthropods, but insects and arachnids are separate classes with different leg counts and body divisions.

questions.stem: Which pair of organisms is most distantly related?
questions.explanation: A fungus and a plant are in different kingdoms. The other pairs share a class or a family.

questions.stem: Which observation would place an unknown animal outside the vertebrates?
options: It has an external skeleton and no internal backbone
questions.explanation: The backbone is the defining feature. Aquatic, egg-laying and legless vertebrates all exist.

questions.stem: A field guide gives both a common and a scientific name for each bird. Why include both?
options: Scientific names are only for experts to check
The two names describe different birds
Common names are familiar to readers, scientific names are unambiguous
questions.explanation: Each does a job the other cannot: recognition versus precision.

questions.stem: Which change to a key step would make it more reliable?
options: Replacing 'large or small' with a measured size range
Adding a third option to the step
questions.explanation: Vague comparatives depend on what the user has seen before. A stated threshold — 'body longer than 15 mm' — is repeatable.

questions.stem: Why do biologists classify bacteria separately from all other single-celled organisms?
options: Bacteria have no nucleus, which is a fundamental cell-level difference
questions.explanation: The prokaryote/eukaryote split is the deepest division in cell structure. Size and lifestyle are secondary.

questions.stem: Which statement about classification and evolution is correct?
options: Classification records evolution but cannot predict it
Classification is based only on how useful organisms are
Modern classification aims to reflect evolutionary relationships
questions.explanation: Groups are intended to reflect shared ancestry, which is why DNA evidence can force a regrouping.

questions.stem: A newly sequenced fungus turns out to be more closely related to animals than to plants. How should this be treated?
options: As a reason to classify on appearance instead, since the molecular data conflicts with what is visible
As an anomaly to set aside, since fungi were grouped with plants long before sequencing was available
As consistent with existing evidence — fungi and animals do share a more recent common ancestor than fungi and plants
As proof the kingdoms should be merged, since shared ancestry means the groups are not really distinct
questions.explanation: This is a well-established result. It is a good illustration of why appearance is a poor guide to relatedness.

questions.stem: Why does adding a newly discovered species sometimes require redrawing a whole group?
options: New species are always placed alone
A species with an unexpected mix of features can show that the group's boundaries were wrong
Every new species creates a new kingdom
Groups must always contain the same number of species
questions.explanation: An intermediate form tests the group definition. If it fits neither side cleanly, the definition was the problem.

questions.stem: Two students key out the same insect and reach different names. What is the best resolution?
options: Assume the key is wrong and stop
Work through the key together, checking the specimen at each step against a reference
questions.explanation: Disagreement almost always traces to one ambiguous step. Retracing it against the specimen finds where the readings diverged.

questions.stem: Why is species richness alone an incomplete measure of biodiversity?
options: It counts only species visible without equipment
It ignores how evenly individuals are spread across those species
It counts individuals rather than species
questions.explanation: A site with 10 species where one dominates is less diverse in practice than one with 10 evenly represented species. Evenness matters alongside richness.

questions.stem: Which piece of evidence would best test whether two isolated populations have become separate species?
options: Counting how many individuals each has
Recording how far apart they live
Bringing them together under controlled conditions and checking for fertile offspring
questions.explanation: The species test is about reproductive compatibility. Distance and size are circumstantial.
